name: Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle
summary: The Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle is a gi blood choke that fuses rear-triangle control of the neck and trapped arm with a deep cross-collar grip and body extension to shear both carotid arteries.
description: Master the Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle in BJJ. Learn collar grip mechanics, leg extension finish, and defensive strategies for this gi technique.
overview:
The Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle combines the structural control of the rear triangle position with the devastating finishing mechanics of the traditional bow and arrow choke. By establishing a triangle lock around the opponent's neck and one arm from behind, the attacker creates a uniquely stable platform that frees both hands for collar manipulation. The rear triangle eliminates many defensive grip-fighting options available against standard bow and arrow setups from back control, making this a particularly high-percentage finishing variation in gi grappling.

The finishing mechanic relies on feeding a deep cross-collar grip behind the opponent's neck while the triangle legs maintain positional control. Once the collar grip is established and the free hand secures the opponent's pants at the knee, the attacker extends their body, arching the back while pulling the collar and straightening the leg grip in opposite directions. This creates a powerful shearing force across the carotid arteries that produces a rapid blood choke.

Strategically, this submission sits at the intersection of two high-control systems: back control through the rear triangle and lapel-based choking through the bow and arrow. The rear triangle provides stability that the traditional bow and arrow from standard back control sometimes lacks, while the bow and arrow adds a devastating finish to a position already rich in submission threats. The trapped arm inside the triangle cannot effectively fight the collar grip, giving the attacker a significant mechanical advantage during setup.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to unconsciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate if released promptly; medical evaluation required if unconsciousness occurs

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from excessive torque and rotation during extension
injury_risks.recovery_time: 3-7 days for minor strain; 2-4 weeks for moderate strain

injury_risks.injury: Jaw or TMJ injury from improper collar placement catching the mandible
injury_risks.recovery_time: 1-3 weeks for minor injury; 4-8 weeks for significant TMJ damage

injury_risks.injury: Knee or hip stress from forced leg extension against resistance

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum to allow tap recognition
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on body or mat
release_protocol: Immediately release collar grip upon tap signal
Release leg extension and triangle lock simultaneously
Allow opponent's head to return to neutral position
If opponent was unconscious, elevate legs and monitor until full recovery
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the choke - apply smooth progressive pressure only
Never use competition-speed extension in training rolls
Always maintain communication with training partner throughout the submission
Never continue pressure after any tap signal is given
Beginners must drill position control and grip placement before attempting the finish
Always allow partner clear access to tap with hands or voice

attacker.name: from Rear Triangle Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to execute the Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle. Step-by-step collar grip setup, leg extension finish, and counter-responses for gi BJJ practitioners.
attacker.overview: Executing the Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle requires maintaining your triangle lock integrity while establishing the deep cross-collar grip and pants control. The rear triangle provides a uniquely stable base since your legs control the opponent's posture and trapped arm, freeing both hands for the collar feed and leg grip that create the bow and arrow finishing mechanic. The key distinction from standard bow and arrow setups is that you already have head and arm control through the triangle, so your focus shifts entirely to grip establishment and the extension finish. The trapped arm inside the triangle cannot effectively interfere with your collar grip, giving you a significant advantage over traditional back control bow and arrow entries where the opponent has both hands free to grip fight.
key_principles: Maintain triangle lock compression while transitioning hands to collar grip - any loosening allows the opponent to extract their trapped arm during setup
Feed the cross-collar grip as deep as possible behind the opponent's neck so the blade of the forearm contacts the carotid rather than catching the jaw
Secure pants grip at the knee on the same side as the collar grip to create opposing force vectors for the finishing extension
Use progressive body extension to finish by arching the back while simultaneously pulling the collar and straightening the leg grip in opposite directions
Time the collar feed during a moment of defensive stillness since attempting the grip while the opponent is actively fighting increases the risk of losing the rear triangle
Keep your choking-side elbow tight against the opponent's neck throughout the extension to prevent the collar from sliding to a less effective position
setup_requirements: Rear triangle fully locked with ankle secured behind the knee and triangle legs compressing the opponent's neck and trapped arm
Opponent's gi collar accessible for cross-grip establishment on the choking side with enough slack to feed deep
Opponent's trapped arm secured inside the triangle to prevent extraction during the collar feed
Chest-to-back connection maintained with hips angled toward the trapped arm side for optimal control
Opponent's posture broken forward to expose the back of the collar for deep grip insertion

execution_steps.action: Confirm and tighten rear triangle lock
execution_steps.description: Verify your triangle is properly locked with your ankle behind your knee and knees squeezed together. The choking leg should cross behind the opponent's neck, not in front. Actively squeeze to compress the space around the trapped arm and remove any slack before releasing your hands from defensive grips.

execution_steps.action: Break posture and expose the collar
execution_steps.description: Use your triangle legs to curl the opponent's posture forward, bringing their chin toward their chest. This exposes the back of their collar and makes the far lapel accessible. Your hands should begin moving toward the collar area once the posture is sufficiently broken and the triangle is bearing the positional control load.

execution_steps.action: Feed the cross-collar grip deep behind the neck
execution_steps.description: Reach your choking hand across the opponent's neck to their far lapel. Thread your four fingers inside the collar as deep as possible so the blade of your wrist sits directly against the side of their neck over the carotid artery. A shallow grip that catches the jaw will produce pain but not an effective blood choke, so prioritize depth over speed.

execution_steps.action: Secure the pants grip at the knee
execution_steps.description: With your free hand, reach down and grip the opponent's pants at the knee on the same side as your collar grip. This grip creates the lever arm needed for the extension finish. Grab the pants material firmly at or just below the knee crease where the fabric bunches, providing a secure handle that will not slip during the extension phase.

execution_steps.action: Begin body extension with controlled pressure
execution_steps.description: Start extending your legs to push the opponent's body away from you while simultaneously pulling the collar grip toward your chest and the pants grip in the opposite direction. The triangle legs provide a fulcrum point at the neck. Extend progressively rather than explosively, allowing your training partner time to recognize the choke and tap safely.

execution_steps.action: Arch and complete the bow and arrow finish
execution_steps.description: Arch your back to maximize the distance between the collar pull and the leg extension, creating the characteristic bow and arrow shape. Your choking forearm blade drives deeper into the carotid as the extension increases. Maintain the triangle squeeze throughout the extension to prevent the opponent from creating rotation or extracting their trapped arm. Hold steady progressive pressure until you receive a tap signal.

execution_steps.action: Monitor for tap and execute release protocol
execution_steps.description: Throughout the extension, stay attentive for verbal or physical tap signals. The blood choke can render an opponent unconscious in 4-8 seconds under full compression, so maintain awareness of their responsiveness. Upon any tap signal or loss of resistance, immediately release the collar grip, unlock the triangle, and allow your partner to recover to a neutral position before checking their status.

common_counters.counter: Two-on-one grip fighting on the collar hand before depth is established
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to strip their grip on your wrist while maintaining triangle compression. If they successfully prevent the collar feed, cycle to rear naked choke or armbar on the trapped arm instead of forcing the bow and arrow.

common_counters.counter: Tucking chin and turning face into the choking forearm to block collar depth
common_counters.your_response: Walk your fingers deeper into the collar incrementally rather than forcing past the chin. Alternatively, use your free hand to cross-face and turn their head away from the choking arm, then immediately re-feed the collar grip to the exposed side of the neck.

common_counters.counter: Rolling toward the collar grip side to relieve extension pressure and invert
common_counters.your_response: Follow the roll by maintaining collar tension and adjusting your body angle. If they complete the roll, you may end up in a top position with the collar grip still intact. Use the pants grip to prevent full rotation and redirect the extension angle.

common_counters.counter: Extracting the trapped arm from the triangle during the collar feed transition
common_counters.your_response: If you feel the arm slipping, immediately re-squeeze the triangle and abandon the collar attempt temporarily. Re-establish full triangle control before attempting the grip again. Consider switching to rear naked choke if the arm comes partially free.

common_errors.error: Loosening the triangle lock while reaching for the collar grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent extracts their trapped arm, eliminating the triangle control and reducing the position to a scramble from back control with weakened hooks
common_errors.correction: Actively squeeze the triangle tighter before releasing your hands. The legs must bear all positional control before you commit both hands to the collar and pants grips.

common_errors.error: Feeding a shallow collar grip that catches the jaw instead of the neck
common_errors.consequence: Creates painful jaw pressure that may get a pain-based tap in training but is ineffective against a determined competitor who will endure it and continue defending
common_errors.correction: Thread fingers deep into the collar past the jawline before closing your grip. The blade of the wrist must contact the carotid artery on the side of the neck for a proper blood choke.

common_errors.error: Extending explosively without progressive pressure application
common_errors.consequence: Risk of neck injury to training partner and potential jaw or TMJ damage from rapid force application before the opponent can recognize and signal a tap
common_errors.correction: Apply the extension gradually over 3-5 seconds. Start with light tension and progressively increase until you feel the opponent tap or the choke is clearly engaged.

common_errors.error: Failing to secure the pants grip before beginning the extension
common_errors.consequence: Without the opposing lever arm, the extension produces less choking force and the opponent can more easily rotate their body to relieve pressure on the carotid
common_errors.correction: Always establish the pants grip at the knee before initiating the extension. Both grips working in opposition create the mechanical advantage that makes the finish effective.

common_errors.error: Losing chest-to-back contact while establishing grips and transitioning to the finish
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for the opponent to rotate, change angle, or begin escape sequences that would be impossible with proper chest pressure maintained
common_errors.correction: Keep your torso pressed against the opponent's back throughout the grip establishment phase. Only create distance during the extension finish once both grips are fully secured.

common_errors.error: Pulling the collar grip perpendicular to the neck instead of along the neck axis
common_errors.consequence: The choking forearm slides off the carotid artery and produces a crank or windpipe pressure rather than an effective blood choke
common_errors.correction: Pull the collar grip diagonally across the neck toward your own hip on the choking side. The force vector should run along the carotid artery, not perpendicular to it.

training_progressions.description: Partner holds rear triangle position statically while you practice feeding the cross-collar grip with proper depth. Focus on getting fingers past the jawline and placing the wrist blade on the carotid. Drill 20 repetitions per side with compliant partner providing feedback on grip depth and placement.

training_progressions.focus: Coordinated collar pull and leg extension
training_progressions.description: With both grips established on a compliant partner, practice the extension finish at 50% intensity. Focus on the simultaneous collar pull and pants push creating opposing forces. Drill the arching motion that maximizes the bow and arrow shape. Partner taps early to build proper pressure sensitivity.

training_progressions.focus: Full technique chain against progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner provides moderate defensive resistance during the collar feed and extension phases. Practice the complete sequence from triangle lock confirmation through the finish. Partner uses grip fighting and chin tucking at 60-70% intensity. Drill transitions to alternative submissions when the bow and arrow is successfully defended.

Start in rear triangle position with full resistance. Attacker works to establish the bow and arrow finish while defender uses all available defensive options. 3-minute rounds with reset after finish or complete escape. Track success rate and identify patterns in defensive responses to refine timing and grip depth.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The choke primarily compresses the carotid arteries on both sides of the neck. The cross-collar grip with the forearm blade presses against one carotid while the triangle leg applies pressure to the opposite carotid. This bilateral compression restricts blood flow to the brain, producing unconsciousness in 4-8 seconds under full compression. The target is arterial blood flow, not the airway.

flashcards.question: What physical indicators tell you the choke is properly applied and approaching the breaking point?
flashcards.answer: The opponent's defensive movements become less coordinated and their grip strength diminishes noticeably. You may feel their body relax incrementally as blood flow restriction takes effect. Their grip-fighting hands slow down or drop away from your collar grip. Skin color changes, particularly reddening of the face and ears, indicate carotid compression is effective. Any loss of resistance requires immediate release and consciousness check.

flashcards.question: What control elements must be established before attempting the collar grip feed?
flashcards.answer: The rear triangle must be fully locked with ankle behind the knee, knees actively squeezing, and the trapped arm pinned securely inside the triangle structure. Chest-to-back connection must be maintained and the opponent's posture should be broken forward. The triangle legs must be bearing the full positional control load before you release your hands to begin the collar feed, since any looseness allows arm extraction.

flashcards.question: At what stage does the Bow and Arrow Choke become extremely difficult for the defender to escape?
flashcards.answer: Once the attacker has established both the deep cross-collar grip behind the neck and the pants grip at the knee, escape becomes extremely difficult. The defender's primary window closes when the collar grip passes the jawline to the neck. After this point, the defender cannot effectively strip the grip with their free hand because the attacker's triangle legs restrict mobility, and the impending extension creates time pressure that limits defensive options.

flashcards.question: What is the most common finishing error and how does it reduce choke effectiveness?
flashcards.answer: The most common error is feeding a shallow collar grip that catches the jawline rather than sitting deep on the carotid artery. This produces a jaw crank that causes pain but does not effectively restrict blood flow to the brain. Experienced competitors can endure jaw pressure and continue defending. The correction is to thread the fingers deep past the jaw and ensure the wrist blade contacts the lateral neck before committing to the extension finish.

flashcards.question: Your initial collar grip is catching the jaw instead of the neck - how do you adjust without losing position?
flashcards.answer: Do not force the extension with a jaw grip. Instead, momentarily loosen the collar grip slightly while using your free hand to cross-face the opponent and turn their chin away from your choking hand. This exposes the neck and allows you to walk your fingers deeper into the collar past the mandible. Once you feel the wrist blade contact the lateral neck, re-secure the pants grip and proceed with the extension. Patience during the grip adjustment prevents jaw injuries.

flashcards.question: What are the critical safety considerations when applying this choke in training?
flashcards.answer: Apply progressive pressure over 3-5 seconds minimum to allow adequate tap recognition time. Never jerk or spike the extension. Monitor training partner's responsiveness continuously since blood chokes can produce unconsciousness in seconds. Release immediately upon any tap signal including verbal, physical hand tap, foot tap, or loss of resistance. After release, check consciousness and allow recovery time. Beginners should drill grip placement without finishing pressure until they develop proper feel and control.

flashcards.question: In competition, how does the scoring context affect your approach to finishing the Bow and Arrow from Rear Triangle?
flashcards.answer: In competition, the rear triangle position already scores 4 points for back control. With points secured, you can methodically work the bow and arrow setup without rushing. Take time to establish the deepest possible collar grip before committing to the extension. If the opponent defends the collar grip effectively, you maintain a dominant scoring position and can cycle to alternative submissions. Never sacrifice the position in a desperate attempt to finish the choke when the points advantage is already secured.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins two-on-one grip fighting your collar hand before you establish depth - what is your response?
flashcards.answer: Use your free hand to strip their top grip on your wrist while maintaining constant triangle compression. If they successfully block the collar feed, do not force it. Instead, switch your attack to the rear naked choke by pulling your choking hand back and threading it under their chin, or transition to attacking the trapped arm with an armbar. The rear triangle provides access to multiple submissions, so cycling between threats is more effective than forcing a defended bow and arrow.

flashcards.question: During the extension finish, your opponent rolls toward the collar grip side to relieve pressure - how do you adjust?
flashcards.answer: Follow the roll by maintaining collar tension and adjusting your body angle to stay behind them. Use the pants grip to resist their rotation and redirect the extension vector. If they complete a partial roll, you may end in a top finishing position with the collar grip intact, which can actually improve your leverage. If they fully invert, be prepared to transition to a modified finishing angle or release and re-establish the rear triangle before they can recover guard position.

defender.name: from Rear Triangle Defender
defender.description: Defend against the Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle. Recognition cues, collar grip defense, escape sequences, and survival tactics for BJJ practitioners.
defender.overview: Defending the Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle requires addressing two simultaneous control systems: the rear triangle lock around your neck and arm, and the collar grip that enables the choking extension. Your primary defensive window occurs during the collar grip establishment phase. Once the attacker has both the deep collar grip and the pants control, escape becomes extremely difficult and the risk of unconsciousness is immediate. Early recognition of the setup and immediate grip fighting on the collar hand are essential for survival. Your trapped arm inside the triangle is largely unavailable for defense, so your free hand must do double duty fighting the collar grip and creating angles for escape. Staying calm and working systematically through defensive priorities gives the best chance of either preventing the finish or escaping to a recoverable position.
key_principles: Fight the collar grip immediately with your free hand before the attacker establishes depth past your jawline - this is your highest priority defensive action
Tuck your chin tightly to your chest and turn your face toward the non-choking side to create a structural barrier against the collar feed
Control the attacker's choking wrist or sleeve with your free hand using a two-on-one grip to prevent the collar from threading deeper
Create rotation toward the collar grip side to reduce the extension angle and prevent the attacker from achieving full bow and arrow leverage
Manage breathing and stay calm despite restricted airway - panicked explosive movements accelerate oxygen depletion and expose you to the finish
Recognize that the pants grip establishment is the final defensive window - once both grips are set, tap immediately rather than risk unconsciousness
recognition_cues: Attacker's hand reaches across your neck toward your far lapel or collar while maintaining the rear triangle lock
You feel fingers threading into your collar behind your neck, indicating the attacker is establishing the cross-collar grip
Attacker's free hand reaches down toward your knee or pants after the collar grip is set, signaling the extension finish is imminent
The triangle pressure changes angle as the attacker adjusts their hips to create the optimal choking line for the bow and arrow extension
Both of the attacker's hands release previous grips simultaneously, indicating they are confident in the triangle control and transitioning to the bow and arrow setup

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one grip strip on the collar hand before depth is established
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the attacker's fingers entering your collar behind your neck, before they close the grip past your jawline
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the choke finish and forces the attacker to re-attempt the collar feed or switch to an alternative submission from the rear triangle
defensive_options.risk: Committing both hands to the collar fight leaves you unable to address the triangle lock or defend against a rapid transition to rear naked choke

defensive_options.action: Chin tuck with head turn toward the non-choking side to create structural barrier
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately upon recognizing the collar feed attempt, as a first-line defense while simultaneously engaging grip fighting
defensive_options.if_successful: Blocks the collar from reaching past the jawline and forces the attacker to adjust their angle, buying time for additional defensive actions
defensive_options.risk: Chin tuck alone is insufficient against a determined attacker who will use the cross-face to turn your head and re-feed the collar

defensive_options.action: Roll toward the collar grip side to reduce extension leverage and work toward guard recovery
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the collar grip is already established and the attacker begins the extension finish - this is a last-resort escape when grip fighting has failed
defensive_options.if_successful: Reduces the choking pressure by shortening the extension distance and may allow you to invert and recover to closed guard or half guard
defensive_options.risk: If the roll is incomplete, the attacker follows and may finish from an even more dominant angle with the collar grip still intact

escape_paths: Strip the collar grip with two-on-one defense and return to rear triangle survival position with active hand fighting to prevent re-establishment
Roll toward the collar grip side during the extension phase while controlling the attacker's wrist to prevent re-gripping, working to recover closed guard
Extract the trapped arm from the triangle structure to eliminate both the positional control and the collar choke threat simultaneously

favorable_outcomes.how: Roll toward the collar grip side during the extension phase to reduce leverage, continue the rotation to invert under the attacker, and use the momentum to recover closed guard with your legs around their waist

Successfully strip the collar grip with two-on-one defense before the attacker can establish depth, forcing them back to the rear triangle position without the bow and arrow threat while you continue working standard rear triangle escapes

common_errors.error: Ignoring the collar grip to focus on escaping the triangle first
common_errors.consequence: The attacker establishes a deep collar grip unopposed and secures the pants grip, making the bow and arrow finish virtually inescapable with unconsciousness likely within seconds
common_errors.correction: Prioritize fighting the collar grip immediately with your free hand. The bow and arrow finish is a more immediate threat than the triangle itself, so address the collar before working triangle escapes.

common_errors.error: Using explosive bridging movements that waste energy without addressing the collar grip
common_errors.consequence: Rapid energy depletion while the attacker maintains both the triangle and collar grip with minimal effort, leaving you exhausted and unable to mount effective defense
common_errors.correction: Use controlled technical movements focused on grip stripping and angle creation rather than explosive attempts to buck the attacker off. Energy conservation is critical for sustained defensive work.

common_errors.error: Continuing to defend after both the collar grip and pants grip are fully established
common_errors.consequence: Risk of unconsciousness from the blood choke before you can execute an escape, especially if the extension compresses both carotids simultaneously
common_errors.correction: Recognize when the position is fully locked in and tap immediately. Once both grips are established and the extension begins, the choke can render you unconscious in 4-8 seconds. Training ego must not override safety.

common_errors.error: Turning the face toward the choking arm side instead of away from it
common_errors.consequence: Exposes the carotid artery directly to the collar grip pressure and accelerates the effectiveness of the blood choke significantly
common_errors.correction: Always turn your face toward the non-choking side and tuck your chin to your chest. This creates a structural barrier that makes it harder for the collar to seat properly on the carotid.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize when the Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle is being set up?
flashcards.answer: The primary cue is feeling the attacker's fingers threading into your collar behind your neck while they maintain the rear triangle lock. You may also notice the attacker releasing their previous grips with both hands simultaneously, indicating confidence in the triangle control. The attacker's hand reaching across your neck toward the far lapel is the most reliable indicator that the bow and arrow setup is beginning rather than other rear triangle submissions.

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the Bow and Arrow Choke from Rear Triangle and what signals should you use?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel the collar grip is deep on your neck and the extension begins with both grips established. Use any available tap signal: verbal tap, physical hand tap on the attacker's body or the mat, or foot tap on the mat. If you feel lightheadedness, vision changes, or tingling, tap immediately regardless of your defensive position. In training, always err on the side of tapping early since this blood choke can produce unconsciousness in seconds.

flashcards.question: What is the highest-priority defensive action when you feel the collar grip being established behind your neck?
flashcards.answer: Immediately use your free hand to grip-fight the attacker's collar hand with a two-on-one strip before they can establish depth past your jawline. Simultaneously tuck your chin to your chest and turn your face away from the choking arm. Speed is critical because once the grip passes the jaw and seats on the carotid, stripping becomes exponentially harder. Every second of delay reduces your defensive options significantly.

flashcards.question: What escape sequence gives you the best chance of reaching closed guard from a partially applied Bow and Arrow?
flashcards.answer: Roll toward the collar grip side while controlling the attacker's collar wrist with your free hand to prevent them from maintaining tension. Use the rolling momentum to invert under the attacker and work your legs around their waist to establish closed guard. This must be timed during the extension phase when the attacker is committing their weight backward, making it harder for them to follow your rotation forward.

flashcards.question: Your opponent has the collar grip but has not yet grabbed your pants - what defensive opportunity does this window provide?
flashcards.answer: This is your critical defensive window because without the pants grip the attacker cannot generate the opposing force needed for the full bow and arrow extension. Focus all effort on stripping the collar grip with your free hand using a two-on-one wrist grip. Simultaneously create rotation by turning your body toward the collar grip side to reduce the angle available for extension. If you can strip the grip now, the attacker must restart the entire setup sequence from the collar feed.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the setup and developing collar grip fighting reflexes
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes rear triangle and slowly initiates the collar feed at 30% speed. Practice recognizing the collar hand entry and responding with immediate two-on-one grip strips. Drill 20 repetitions focusing on reaction time between feeling the collar feed and engaging the defensive grip. Partner provides feedback on defensive timing.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: Escape Sequences Under Controlled Pressure
training_progressions.focus: Rolling escapes and guard recovery mechanics
training_progressions.description: Partner applies the bow and arrow at 50-60% intensity with the collar grip established. Practice the rolling escape toward the collar grip side and guard recovery sequence. Focus on timing the roll during the extension phase and maintaining wrist control throughout. Partner allows the escape if technique is correct but maintains pressure if form breaks down.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance defensive application and tap timing
training_progressions.description: Start in rear triangle with partner working full-speed bow and arrow attempts. Defend using all available options including grip fighting, chin defense, and rolling escapes. Practice recognizing when to tap rather than continuing to defend a fully locked submission. 2-minute rounds with reset after finish or successful escape to guard. Track defensive success rate to measure improvement.
